drills.q: Explain Postgres's xmin/xmax visibility rule precisely.
drills.a: A tuple version is visible to a snapshot if xmin's transaction committed before the snapshot was taken, and either xmax is unset (still live) or xmax's transaction has not committed as of the snapshot. Checked per-tuple during a scan.

drills.q: Why does MVCC let readers never block writers, unlike 2PL?
drills.a: A reader simply reads an older, already-committed row version instead of waiting for the newest write to finish - it never needs a lock on the current version. Writers still conflict with other writers on the same row, but reader-writer blocking is eliminated entirely.

drills.q: Name all six concurrency anomalies with a one-line definition each.
drills.a: Dirty read (uncommitted write visible), dirty write (overwrite an uncommitted write), read skew (same row, two reads in one txn, different answers), phantom read (predicate result set changes mid-txn), lost update (same-row read-modify-write, one write clobbers another), write skew (disjoint rows, writes jointly violate an invariant neither alone violated).

drills.q: Walk through the doctors-on-call write skew example in full, two transactions.
drills.a: Invariant: >=1 doctor on call. Alice's txn reads count=2 from its snapshot, decides safe to go off-call, updates Alice's row, commits. Bob's txn concurrently reads count=2 from its own snapshot, decides safe, updates Bob's row, commits. Final count=0. No write-write conflict was ever detected because the two updates touched different rows.

drills.q: Why does snapshot isolation stop read skew but not write skew, mechanically?
drills.a: Read skew is prevented directly because a fixed snapshot gives internally consistent repeated reads. Write skew is a violated cross-transaction invariant caused by disjoint writes - SI's conflict detection only checks for same-row write-write conflicts, which never occurs in write skew since the rows written are different.

drills.q: Give the real default isolation level for Postgres, MySQL, Oracle, and SQL Server.
drills.a: Postgres, Oracle, SQL Server: Read Committed. MySQL/InnoDB: Repeatable Read (with gap locks suppressing most phantoms beyond the ANSI minimum).

drills.q: Is Oracle's SERIALIZABLE actually serializable? What's the practical consequence?
drills.a: No - Oracle's SERIALIZABLE is snapshot isolation under a different name; it implements neither SSI nor 2PL-style predicate locking. Write skew remains possible on Oracle SERIALIZABLE, so you must add explicit row locking (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE) to actually protect a cross-row invariant.

drills.q: Explain how Postgres's SSI detects write skew without blocking any reader.
drills.a: SERIALIZABLE transactions take non-blocking SIREAD locks on data they read. A later write to SIREAD-covered data creates an rw-antidependency edge. A cycle of two such edges through a pivot transaction (a dangerous structure) triggers a serialization failure, aborting one transaction for retry - all without ever blocking a read.

drills.q: An account balance goes negative despite a CHECK(balance >= 0) constraint and every individual UPDATE looking correct. Diagnose.
drills.a: Lost update or write skew between two concurrent balance-modifying transactions under Read Committed or Snapshot Isolation. A single-row CHECK constraint can't catch a cross-row/cross-transaction invariant violation. Fix: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE before computing the new value, or run at SERIALIZABLE and handle retries.

drills.q: Design the fix for a flight-booking system where two transactions might both book the last seat.
drills.a: Best: atomic conditional UPDATE flights SET seats_available = seats_available - 1 WHERE id=? AND seats_available > 0, checking the affected-row count - folds check-then-write into one atomic statement, no separate stale read. Alternatives: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE before deciding, or SERIALIZABLE with retry handling.

drills.q: Why do predicate locks matter, and what happens under pure 2PL without them?
drills.a: Row locks alone only guard rows that existed when the lock was taken - a newly inserted row matching the same query condition slips through unnoticed (a phantom). Predicate locks lock the range/condition itself, catching new matching rows too.

drills.q: What operational risk comes from XID wraparound, and what prevents it?
drills.a: 32-bit XIDs wrap every ~4 billion transactions; ambiguity in xmin comparisons could cause data corruption. Autovacuum's freeze rewrites old tuples' xmin to a frozen sentinel. An under-vacuumed high-write table risks Postgres forcing read-only mode as the counter approaches the limit.

drills.q: When would you choose SELECT ... FOR UPDATE over running the whole transaction at SERIALIZABLE?
drills.a: When you know exactly which rows back the invariant and want to pay locking cost only there, rather than SIREAD bookkeeping and a higher retry rate across the whole transaction. Risk: missing one of the dangerous reads silently reintroduces the anomaly with no warning - SERIALIZABLE doesn't require hand-enumerating them.

drills.q: Why does MySQL choose a stronger default isolation level (Repeatable Read) than Postgres/Oracle/SQL Server (Read Committed)?
drills.a: Historically tied to statement-based replication needing more deterministic read behavior to replay correctly across replicas - Repeatable Read's stronger per-transaction snapshot consistency reduced a class of replication correctness bugs that Read Committed's per-statement snapshot would have made harder to reason about.
